title: Normalized scope model and admin guardrails for RBAC v2
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description: Summary: Define a normalized RBAC v2 role model that standardizes resource hierarchy, scope normalization, and permission tiers, plus concrete admin guardrails and audit logging contract. This ticket covers the design proposal, migration strategy from RBAC v1, SSO/SAML group-to-role sync semantics, and a rollout/checklist for canary and full rollouts. Goal: produce an unambiguous role-scope-permission contract that can be implemented by the authorization service and enforced by dataplane components (console/API/runtime).
background: Why this matters: Current RBAC is flat and ad-hoc across tenants. We have several operational gaps: unclear ownership of admin roles, inconsistent scope naming across services, and audit logs that lack decision provenance for automated troubleshooting. As Redwood supports more Dedicated/Private customers and third-party SSO, we must ship a stable RBAC v2 that supports hierarchical resource scoping, deterministic permission resolution, and strong auditability without regressing latency targets.
goals: 1) Define canonical resource hierarchy and normalized scope strings. 2) Establish permission tier semantics (view, operate, manage, owner). 3) Design admin guardrails (break-glass, least-privilege defaults, delegated admin boundaries). 4) Specify audit log schema for authorization decisions. 5) Document SSO/SAML role mapping and group sync behaviour. 6) Provide migration steps and safe rollout plan.
non_goals: We are not implementing datastore migration or the enforcement hooks in this ticket. Integration tests with runtime are separate tickets. This is the design and rollout plan only.
design_notes:
Key decisions and trade-offs considered:

- Scope normalization: use a canonical slash-delimited resource path: <resource_type>:<region?>/<tenant_id>/<namespace?>/<resource_id?>. Examples: 'project/us-west/tenant-42/dataset-13' or 'org/enterprise-acme/team-ml'. We avoid freeform labels because they break deterministic ACL resolution.

- Permission tiers: four core canonical verbs mapped to capabilities: 'view' (read-only, list/detail), 'operate' (perform actions but not modify config), 'manage' (create/update/delete), 'owner' (full admin incl. role binding). These map to internal action sets rather than raw endpoints to make policy stable across API changes.

- Inheritance semantics: child scopes inherit parent grants unless explicitly blocked by a deny tag. Inheritance is transitive. We adopt deny precedence when decision evaluation hits explicit denies. This simplifies reasoning for tenant admins while allowing global guards.

- Admin guardrails: default global admin role is disabled for hosted customers. Instead, we use an 'Org-Owner' pattern: org owners can grant roles within their org scope; cross-org elevation requires explicit break-glass with two-person approval and audit annotation. Break-glass generates a time-limited token and an immutable audit event containing decision_id, approver_ids, justification, and TTL.

- SSO/SAML mapping: support two modes: group sync (periodic, authoritative) and Just-In-Time (JIT) mapping (attribute-based on assertion). Group sync writes derived role bindings into RBAC service; JIT evaluates attributes at login without persisting derived bindings. We recommend group sync for enterprise customers doing long-lived role assignments and JIT for transient session attributes.

- Audit contract: every authorization decision must emit a structured audit event with these fields: timestamp, request_id, principal_id, principal_type, decision_id, evaluated_scope, matching_role_ids, matched_rules, decision (allow/deny), reason, cache_hit (true/false), evaluation_latency_ms, and trace_id. Events must be URL-safe JSON strings in our audit pipeline and retained per compliance settings.

- Latency trade-offs: full policy resolution can be expensive with deep inheritance. We plan an index of direct bindings per normalized-scope and a cached materialized policy for hot tenants. Cache invalidation must be per-binding change to keep correctness. If cache misses, decision falls back to authoritative evaluation and event emits cache_hit=false.
permission_matrix:
CSV:
resource_scope,role,view,operate,manage,owner,notes
org/*,Org-Viewer,true,false,false,false,read-only across org
org/*,Org-Operator,true,true,false,false,operate across org-level runtime operations
org/*,Org-Admin,true,true,true,false,manage org config but cannot grant global admin
org/*,Org-Owner,true,true,true,true,can bind roles within org scope
org/tenant-*/project/*,Project-Reader,true,false,false,false,read-only project resources
org/tenant-*/project/*,Project-Editor,true,true,true,false,modify project artifacts
org/tenant-*/project/*,Project-Admin,true,true,true,false,grant roles inside project
*/*,Global-Audit,true,false,false,false,read-only access to audit streams (subject to audit RBAC)
examples:
- Example 1: Service A attempts `dataset.read` in 'org/tenant-42/project/p1/dataset/d7'. Evaluation finds binding at 'org/tenant-42' with role Project-Reader => allow (view=true). Audit event includes decision_id and matched_rules.
- Example 2: User requests role-binding creation across orgs. System denies unless Org-Owner present or break-glass flow used. Break-glass requires 2 approvers, logs approver IDs and TTL.
- Example 3: SAML assertion contains attribute 'x-redwood-role=Project-Editor' and 'group=ml-team'. In JIT mode, user session carries elevated rights mapped to that scope for session duration; in group-sync mode, RBAC service persists binding 'Project-Editor -> org/tenant-42/project/p1' during provisioning.
migration_plan: Phase 1: Publish canonical naming and translation rules (this ticket). Phase 2: Backfill existing bindings into normalized scope store for a pilot tenant set; create materialized policy cache for top 100 tenants. Phase 3: Enable new decision engine behind a feature flag and run in parallel (shadow) for 2 weeks comparing decisions to v1. Phase 4: Remediate mismatches, update tests, then flip canary for non-production tenants. Phase 5: Full rollout with opt-in period. Rollback plan: revert to v1 by routing decisions to legacy service while continuing to accept new bindings in the normalized format; record a migration delta for reconciliation.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Design doc approved by Security and SRE. 2) Audit schema accepted and example events validated in the audit pipeline. 3) Migration plan describes backfill queries and safe toggles. 4) SSO/SAML mapping modes documented with sample assertions and provisioning steps. 5) Performance budget defined: average auth decision 95th percentile < 18ms for cached tenants, < 60ms uncached. 6) Test vectors and unit test list produced.
rollout_checklist:
- [ ] Security review complete
- [ ] Conformance tests for deny precedence
- [ ] Audit event consumer accepts new schema
- [ ] Cache invalidation unit tests
- [ ] SSO group sync scripts for pilot customers
- [ ] Break-glass UI/flow spec delivered
- [ ] Monitoring dashboard: decision latency, cache hit rate, audit event volume
- [ ] Post-rollout incident runbook
monitoring_metrics: decision_latency_p50_ms, decision_latency_p95_ms, policy_cache_hit_rate, audit_events_per_minute, break_glass_activations, role_binding_changes_per_minute
testing_plan:
- Unit tests for scope normalization and comparator.
- Integration tests that simulate inheritance and deny rules across 3 levels of scope.
- Load test: evaluate decision service at 5k reqs/sec with 90% cache hit.
- Regression test: compare v1 vs v2 decisions across 2000 historical auth logs (shadow).
- SSO tests: SAML assertion mapping (JIT and group sync), expired assertion handling.
risks_and_mitigations:
Risk: Incorrect translation causes privilege escalation. Mitigation: shadow run with detailed diffs, small pilot and manual review of top mismatches.
Risk: Audit volume increase leads to higher storage costs. Mitigation: tiered retention and sampling for low-risk events; full retention per compliance settings.
Risk: Cache invalidation bugs causing stale permissions. Mitigation: event-driven invalidation, per-binding versioning, and conservative TTL fallback.
